item.title: Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips
item.description: arXiv:2610.14244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips. Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant. Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop. Our results have important implications for HBM-based system design and validation. Relying solely on JEDEC- or vendor-specified test loops to bound HBM power could cause system failures and/or thermal throttling in real-world high-power AI/ML workloads. To improve 3D-stacked DRAM power modeling in open source architectural simulation infrastructures, we develop a new HBM power model. Our model predicts the power of 36 real HBM2 chips across diverse workloads (including a real LLM decode workload) with 7.6 -- 8.1% mean absolute percentage error, substantially more accurately than state-of-the-art HBM power models. The power consumption predicted by our model for a power-intensive microbenchmark closely matches (with 2.4% to 5.3% error across HBM3E's specified supply voltage range) the average HBM3E memory power consumed by three tested NVIDIA H200 GPUs. We publicly release our power model at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HBM-Power.
item.dc:creator: Ataberk Olgun, Spiros Galanopoulos, Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris, \.Ismail Emir Y\"uksel, Haocong Luo, F. Nisa Bostanc{\i}, Onur Mutlu

item.title: DFIT: A Framework for Building Instrumentation Tools Across Heterogeneous Dataflow Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2610.14280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emerging dataflow accelerators offer exceptional energy efficiency and throughput for machine learning workloads, yet remain largely opaque to developers for performance analysis. Unlike CPUs and GPUs, where instrumentation frameworks enable fine-grained introspection, dataflow hardware exposes little information. This lack of transparency limits the ability of compiler engineers, system designers, and application developers to analyze, tune, or debug accelerator behavior. In this paper, we introduce DFIT (DataFlow Accelerator Instrumentation Tool), an instrumentation framework designed specifically for dataflow architectures. DFIT directly instruments operations, regions, and compiler transformations at the graph IR and backend-lowering stages using semantic program representation. DFIT captures high-level, semantically meaningful data that reflect the true dataflow of computation. These data can be exported for visualization and analysis. Our approach demonstrates how instrumentation can be generalized beyond traditional hardware to support heterogeneous architectures, providing portability without modifying tool logic. By opening the black box of dataflow execution, DFIT establishes a foundation for new classes of performance analysis tools for AI accelerators. It provides a practical path toward reproducible, architecture-aware introspection across heterogeneous systems, bridging the long-standing visibility gap between compiler design, runtime scheduling, and hardware realization. Evaluation across Cerebras, SambaNova, and TPU shows practical overhead of 3.53%-13.62% across instrumentation modes with robust cross-platform portability.
item.dc:creator: Md. Azahar Alam, Abrar Hossain, Kishwar Ahmed

item.title: HADES: A Programmable Processing-Near-Memory Engine for Binary Similarity Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.14677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moving operands to a processor can cost more than the arithmetic performed on them, and for small binary similarity and search workloads data movement can dominate. We present HADES, a programmable processing-near-memory engine built around one shared 32x32-bit 2R1W register-file macro that holds both data and program. Twelve 16-bit opcodes, three working registers and a 32-slot program express ten search workloads in 8 to 19 slots, and SCANP and SCANSEL shorten dual-row and selected scans. A post-layout 2x2 Tiny Tapeout implementation closes timing at 40 MHz with 26,968 square microns of standard cells beside a 15,744 square microns macro. All HADES results come from RTL or gate-level simulation of this implementation, and HADES energy is estimated. Against ESP8266 and ESP32 microcontrollers running plain C, and with an ideal host, HADES answers a resident query 10x to 32x and 2.2x to 11x faster, respectively. End to end, it wins at the evaluated batch sizes of B = 16 and B = 256 against both boards and loses the single-query (B = 1) runs to the ESP32. An Arduino Nano runs a restricted subset. Kernel power stays within about 2% of a spin loop on all three boards. These results hold for plain-C baselines under the evaluated conditions. At this scale the control and instruction storage fit around a shared memory macro, while the byte-wide interface and the loading path remain significant costs.
item.dc:creator: Pranav M

item.title: "Is Low Power Enough?" Rethinking Energy Efficiency in High-Fidelity Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2610.14714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For two decades, long-lived sensor nodes have been built from the lowest-power parts, because their scalar readings take only milliseconds to acquire and send. Scientists now want higher fidelity data from the field, such as images and audio, and these observations break that rule: a low-power microcontroller stays awake for seconds to read, store, and transmit each one, so low power is no longer low energy. We argue that long-lived, high-fidelity nodes should instead be built around a more capable microcontroller, provided the whole board sleeps deeply. We revisit two principles from early sensor networks, "race to sleep" and "talk less", for high-fidelity data and on-device AI, and test them by comparing the STM32N6, which pairs a fast core with a neural accelerator, against the low-power Apollo4 Plus. Although the STM32N6 draws 1.9x more power, it completes an observation (capture, storage, on-board detection, and a LoRa transmission) 9.9x faster and so uses 5.2x less energy. On the same model, it runs inference with 3.2-11.4x less energy, and it fits models over 23 points more accurate. A high-fidelity node lives longest when it finishes quickly, sleeps deeply, and sends only what matters.
item.dc:creator: Chae Young Lee, Lan Mei, Jesse Fonseca, Zerina Kapetanovic

item.title: GaborFlow: Hardware-Software Co-Optimization of Gabor Filter Accelerator Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.15003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brain tumor classification from MRI scans represents a critical challenge in medical imaging, where accuracy directly impacts patient outcomes. This paper introduces GaborFlow, a novel hardware-software co-optimization framework that revolutionizes the design of the Gabor Filter accelerator for generating feature maps to enhance brain tumor detection. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on fixed filter parameters, our method employs trainable Gabor coefficients within a carefully optimized range, integrated with an EfficientNet-B0 backbone CNN architecture. The innovation lies in the synergistic combination of software optimization through Bayesian hyperparameter tuning and hardware efficiency through precision-optimized multipliers. Our GF baseline accelerator achieves remarkable results, with 98.6% classification accuracy, 28.08% power benefits, and 48.83% footprint savings compared to state-of-the-art implementations, demonstrating that medical AI can be both highly accurate and energy-efficient. The hardware design files are made freely available for easy adoption and further usage by the researchers and designers.
item.dc:creator: Priyanka Agarwal, Pruthvi Parate, Raghav Khurana, Madhav Rao

item.title: Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Cole Strickler, Renato Mancuso, Manos Athanassoulis, Heechul Yun

item.title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.
item.dc:creator: Shiva Ahir, Hashmath Shaik, Alex Doboli, Nadeem Yaseen, Simona Doboli

item.title: The Era of Vibe Tapeout: Dark Age or Golden Age for Analog Circuit Design?
item.description: arXiv:2610.15240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents now write their own schematic and layout generators, run EDA tools, read the results, and fix the design. This "vibe tapeout" is becoming practical for analog circuits as well. This paper measures how far it has come in two settings. (A) On an open PDK (SKY130), a cloud LLM agent designed an 11-bit, 5.12-MS/s SAR ADC from its specification. The agents produced DRC- and LVS-clean macros and met the specification after parasitic extraction (PEX). In particular, under the condition in which the agent received a sanitized reference design derived from our 65-nm design (vibe porting), it produced the best layout in the shortest time. Its area was 1/1.6 to 1/2.8 of that of the conditions without a reference. This condition reached signoff without human intervention. The agents also identified the causes of post-PEX degradation (CDAC wiring coupling and common-mode-dependent comparator offset) by their own experiments. On the other hand, agents sometimes reported false passes, and verification independent of the design agent was essential. (B) A commercial PDK is under NDA and cannot be given to a cloud LLM. We therefore evaluated local LLMs running on university servers with a six-task benchmark on a commercial 65-nm CMOS PDK. Kimi K3 passed five of the six tasks, while MiniMax M3 passed two. Neither solved the debugging task, which requires finding the cause from symptoms. Finally, we discuss the prospects for extending vibe tapeout from ADCs to entire SoCs, and ask whether vibe tapeout is a dark age or a golden age for analog design. Our answer is that it is a golden age for designers who know what to verify.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Yoshioka

item.title: Stateless Stochastic Computing for Generative AI on Superconducting Logic: A Model-Hardware Co-Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.15392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic computing lets stochastic physical dynamics carry out a computation and reads out the result as a time average. Recently, thermodynamic computing has been demonstrated on several hardware platforms, including digital CMOS circuits based on stochastic computing. Superconducting single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic offers very high clock rates and very low switching energy, but it heavily penalizes state, memory, fan-out, and feedback, i.e., exactly the per-neuron accumulators on which such designs rely. We therefore realize thermodynamic computing in SFQ logic through a co-design of a generative model and its circuit in which the datapath holds no state at all. The model is a class-conditional flow-matching image generator, which transforms Gaussian noise into an image of the requested class along a short, deterministic path of four Euler steps; in hardware, these steps are unrolled into a feed-forward pipeline of stochastic bitstream operators, whose output is read out as a time average, as in thermodynamic computing, without any relaxation phase. Each layer of the model is a butterfly-factorized linear map built exclusively from multiplexers that operate on split-unipolar bitstreams. The ReLU activation, which in stochastic computing requires a per-neuron up/down counter (accounting for 60-70% of the JJs in a counter-based design), is replaced by a stateless AND-NOT gate whose one-clock input skew is provided at no cost by SFQ gate-level pipelining. The models are trained directly on the stream representation of the hardware, with a regularizer that bounds the stream gains. Synthesis with an SFQ design flow shows that stochastic streams tolerate relaxed path balancing, which reduces the Josephson-junction (JJ) count of a hard-wired stage by 40-47%.
item.dc:creator: Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

item.title: Integration, Enhancements and Evaluation of Memory Simulators
item.description: arXiv:2610.15873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Currently, there is no common methodology or set of practices for evaluating memory-system performance in integrated simulation infrastructures. As a result, studies adopt different evaluation approaches, which can lead to conflicting conclusions even for the same simulation infrastructure. We propose a validation methodology that evaluates memory-system performance from three complementary views: the memory simulator, the CPU--memory interface and the simulated application. We use these views to detect, understand and correct memory-simulation inaccuracies arising from simulator integration and simplified modeling of microarchitectural features. The methodology reveals that the application's perception of memory performance can become effectively decoupled from the detailed memory simulation. Most importantly, we identify and correct a fundamental memory-model mismatch between delayed-response cycle-accurate memory simulators and ZSim, a representative parallel CPU simulator. We demonstrate the broader applicability of these enhancements by applying them to ZSim integrations with Ramulator 2, DRAMsim3 and DRAMSys 4, covering all major public cycle-accurate memory simulators. After the corrections and enhancements, all integrations reproduce the main bandwidth--latency trends and key characteristics of the actual system. Across the evaluated simulators, STREAM bandwidth differs from actual-hardware measurements by less than 5% in most experiments, while pointer-chase latency remains 15--18% lower than on actual hardware. All simulator enhancements are released as open source.
item.dc:creator: Pouya Esmaili-Dokht, Arash Yadegari, Victor Xirau, Julian Pavon, Hamid Sarbazi-Azad, Adri\'an Cristal, Eduard Ayguad\'e, Petar Radojkovi\'c

item.title: GarageWorks: A Shared Testbench Abstraction for Software Simulation and FPGA Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.15925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GarageWorks is a lightweight FPGA testing framework that enables the same cocotb testbench to be used for both software RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated hardware simulation. A shared abstraction hides backend-specific interfaces, while synthesizable Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) dispatchers provide design-under-test (DUT)-specific control and test operations on the FPGA. GarageWorks is intended for rapid bare-metal testing of standalone designs and on-chip processing logic for scientific sensors, rather than full SoC-level prototyping. The framework has been validated on AMD Alveo V80 FPGAs with several internal designs and provides initial support for AI-assisted generation of DUT-specific test components.
item.dc:creator: Kazutomo Yoshii

item.title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.16159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.
item.dc:creator: Gang Liu, Chen Yang, Junyan Hu, Jianguo Chen, Lixin Duan

item.title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
item.description: arXiv:2610.16213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.
item.dc:creator: Fatemeh Bahrami, Seyed-Hosein Attarzadeh-Niaki

item.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.16890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
item.dc:creator: Chanyoung Moon, Travis Pence, Daisuke Yamada, Jiaqi Mo, Yanxin Zhang, Vikas Singh, Karthikeyan Sankaralingam

item.title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
item.description: arXiv:2610.17099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Ding, Xuanyu Liang, Xinyang Liu, Boyang Li, Zhiqiang Que, Guosheng Hu, Jiayang Li

item.title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
item.description: arXiv:2610.17445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.
item.dc:creator: Bodong Hou, Zhixin Pan

item.title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
item.description: arXiv:2610.17449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.
item.dc:creator: Chengjia Liu, Priyadarsi Mishra, David Kebo Houngninou, Michael Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, Jiang Hu

item.title: FPGA Based Design And Implementation of Neural Network Compensators for Nanocrystalline MEMS Pressure Sensor
item.description: arXiv:2610.18136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper the effects of nonlinearity and temperature of nanocrystalline MEMS pressure sensor have been compensated using neural network algorithm which has been implemented on a FPGA chip. The neural network employs back propagation algorithm to train the multilayer perceptron feed forward network that causes an error reduction due to temperature upto the level of 98%. It is realized on FPGA with pipelined architecture for parallel and fast sensing operation. The pressure sensor along with the FPGA based compensation results in an intelligent sensor system capable of high speed and accurate pressure measurement which has been tested for a typical biomedical application.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: VSI, TEQIP, DIT sponsored national conference on Design Techniques for modern electronic devices, VLSI and Communication Systems (DTVC- 2007) at NIT Hamirpur ,Himachal Pradesh, India
item.dc:creator: Somsubhra Talapatra, Sudip Ghosh, C Roy Chaudhuri, Biplab K Sikdar, Hafizur Rahaman

item.title: Comparative Robustness of Mach-Zehender and Microring Photonic Matrix Multipliers Under Laser RIN and Thermal Drift
item.description: arXiv:2610.15400v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Photonic matrix multipliers can accelerate neural-network inference, but their practical utility depends on how optical weight elements respond to source noise, thermal variation, and calibration error. This paper compares Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) and microring-resonator (MRR) implementations under laser relative-intensity noise (RIN), column-wise thermal/phase drift, and their joint action. Two CIFAR-10 classifiers - a compact four-layer CNN and ResNet-8 - are mapped to matched photonic multiply-accumulate chains using common source-distribution, detection, numerical, and calibration assumptions. Both architectures reproduce the same zero-perturbation baseline for each workload: 79.5% classification accuracy for the Small CNN and 70.0% for ResNet-8. Robustness is then evaluated using separate RIN-only and drift-only sweeps and a full two-dimensional RIN-drift grid, with dimensionless RMS perturbation levels extending from 0.5% to 20%. The analysis reports classification accuracy, class normalized confusion matrices, rolling-accuracy traces, one-dimensional robustness curves, and multidimensional response surfaces. Device equations and parameter definitions follow the models implemented in the QPI Labs Photonic Inference Simulator, with shared laser fluctuations propagated as correlated multiplicative noise and slow drift represented as a per-output-column perturbation of calibrated weights. All numerical results are generated from recorded experiment configurations and random seeds. The study provides a controlled system-level framework for comparing interferometric and resonant photonic weight elements while limiting conclusions to the implemented device models, perturbation ranges, calibration policy, and neural-network workloads.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Falkenberg

item.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.15781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.
item.dc:creator: Cameron Barker, Andreas Paraskeva, Jan N. van Rijn, Elliot J. Crowley, Henry Gouk

item.title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
item.description: arXiv:2610.16373v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Shakiba, Hamid Reza Ghaeini, Sadegh Dorri Nogoorani

item.title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.18391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.
item.dc:creator: Mayank Kabra, Phillip Widdowson, Harshita Gupta, Rakesh Nadig, Nisa Bostanc{\i}, Eirini Tzermpou, Rakesh Kumar, Spiros Galanopoulos, Ataberk Olgun, Abdullah Giray Ya\u{g}l{\i}k\c{c}{\i}, Mohammad Sadrosadati, Onur Mutlu

item.title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2610.18641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $\mu$W.
item.dc:creator: Dhairya Shah, Rajashekar Reddy Chinthalapani, Pramuka Sooriya Patabandige, Ambuj Varshney

item.title: Low Cost C-ITS Stations Using Raspberry Pi and the Open Source Software OScar
item.description: arXiv:2503.15461v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The deployment of cooperative-intelligent transport systems (C-ITS) has started, and standardization and research activities are moving forward to improve road safety and vehicular efficiency. An aspect that is still felt as a limitation by the research groups active in the field, is the difficulty to validate the solutions with real hardware and software, because of the huge investments that are needed when multiple equipped vehicles need to be considered. In this work, we present a platform with low-cost hardware based on a Raspberry Pi and a Wi-Fi module transmitting at 5.9 GHz, and on the open-source software Open Stack for Car (OScar), which is compliant with the ETSI C-ITS standards. With a limited cost in the order of 200 EUR, the platform realizes a device which is standard compliant and can be used as either on-board unit (OBU) or road side unit (RSU). The limited cost makes the testbed scalable to several units with limited budget and the limited size makes it also deployable on mini-cars to test advanced connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) networks and applications. Our tests demonstrate its interoperability with other devices, compliance in terms of power spectrum, and a range of a few hundred meters in line-of-sight (LOS) conditions using the standard settings of ITS-G5.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Farina, Matteo Piccoli, Salvatore Iandolo, Antonio Solida, Carlo Augusto Grazia, Francesco Raviglione, Claudio Casetti, Alessandro Bazzi

item.title: FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerators for Space Applications: A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2504.16173v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space missions are becoming increasingly ambitious, necessitating high-performance onboard spacecraft computing systems. In response, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) have garnered significant interest due to their flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and radiation tolerance potential. Concurrently, neural networks (NNs) are being recognized for their capability to execute space mission tasks such as autonomous operations, sensor data analysis, and data compression. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to implement FPGA-based NN accelerators in space applications. By analyzing existing literature, identifying trends and gaps, and proposing future research directions, this work highlights the potential of these accelerators to enhance onboard computing systems.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Antunes, Artur Podobas

item.title: RISC-Q: A Generator for Real-Time Quantum Control System-on-Chips Compatible with RISC-V
item.description: arXiv:2505.14902v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum computing imposes stringent requirements for the precise control of large-scale qubit systems, including, for example, microsecond-latency feedback and nanosecond-precision timing of gigahertz signals-demands that far exceed the capabilities of conventional real-time systems. The rapidly evolving and highly diverse nature of quantum control necessitates the development of specialized hardware accelerators. While a few custom real-time systems have been developed to meet the tight timing constraints of specific quantum platforms, they face major challenges in scaling and adapting to increasingly complex control demands-largely due to fragmented toolchains and limited support for design automation. To address these limitations, we present RISC-Q---an open-source flexible generator for Quantum Control System-on-Chip (QCSoC) designs, featuring a programming interface compatible with the RISC-V ecosystem. Developed using SpinalHDL, RISC-Q enables efficient automation of highly parameterized and modular QCSoC architectures, supporting agile and iterative development to meet the evolving demands of quantum control. We demonstrate that RISC-Q can replicate the performance of existing QCSoCs with significantly reduced development effort, facilitating efficient exploration of the hardware-software co-design space for rapid prototyping and customization.
item.dc:creator: Junyi Liu, Yi Lee, Haowei Deng, Connor Clayton, Gengzhi Yang, Xiaodi Wu

item.title: LowRank-SSM: Hardware-Software Co-Design for Rank-Reduced Mamba Acceleration on FPGA
item.description: arXiv:2608.02954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba and Mamba-2 achieve linear-time autoregressive inference, making them attractive for latency-sensitive and resource-constrained deployment. Yet every generated token still reads the full input and output projection weights of every layer from off-chip memory, and on an FPGA these two projections take the majority of a layer's cycles. Existing accelerators lower this cost by quantizing the weights or by speeding up the scan, but none reduce the number of weight elements a token must read, and a low-rank factorization on its own does not help: without a datapath built for it, the two-stage product takes as long as the dense one. We present \textbf{LowRank-SSM}, a hardware-software co-design framework that jointly addresses three constraints of rank-reduced Mamba inference: where rank should be spent, how the resulting factors should execute, and how reduced weight traffic should be delivered by the FPGA memory system. A sensitivity-guided per-projection search allocates rank under a perplexity ceiling while restricting compression to Mamba-2 operands that tolerate approximation. A rank-configurable projection datapath maps both factor stages onto the existing GEMV engines, keeping the intermediate vector on chip and changing rank through loop bounds and weight images rather than bitstream recompilation. A platform-aware NoC/AXI memory subsystem then balances and prefetches weight streams to sustain 42\,GB/s. Together, these software and hardware choices convert structural rank reduction into measured latency reduction: in our ablation, 93\% of the projection traffic removed by rank reduction appears as saved token latency. With a rank schedule found under a 5\% perplexity ceiling, which costs 1.6 points of average zero-shot accuracy, the complete accelerator decodes Mamba2-2.7B at 16.79 tokens/s and 0.41\,J per token.
item.dc:creator: Haocheng Xu, Yu-an Chou, Bhardwaj Bhat, Zhiheng Chen, Ye Qiao, Yifan Zhang, Leyao Han, Saptarshi Mitra, Sitao Huang

item.title: NOVA-CIM: Noise- and Correlation-Tolerant Stochastic Interfaces for Analog Compute-in-Memory
item.description: arXiv:2609.07059v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient model acceleration, but its reliance on ADC-based readout, which directly quantizes noisy column currents, makes inference accuracy highly sensitive to analog read noise, active-row scaling, and ADC precision. In this paper, we present NOVA-CIM, a noise- and correlation-tolerant stochastic interface for analog CIM by replacing multi-bit ADC readout with random-reference 1-bit sensing and reconstructing results through lightweight counting. By converting column currents into comparison probabilities, this probability-domain readout averages zero-mean dynamic read noise over stochastic samples while reducing dependence on high-resolution ADCs. We provide a unified robustness analysis showing that dynamic read noise is suppressed through temporal averaging and that spatial input-bitstream correlation increases instantaneous current variance rather than introducing first-order MAC bias. MAC-level experiments and end-to-end evaluation on ViT-Base validate the analysis: under read noise, Top-1 accuracy remains 84.48% near the 84.51% bfloat16 (BF16) baseline; under stochastic number generator (SNG) reuse, MAC bias stays near zero while root-mean-square error (RMSE) and stochastic cross-correlation (SCC) grow as predicted.
item.dc:creator: Jiachen Ren, Wenshuai Yao, Haobo Liu, Xincheng Feng, Chenxi Hu, Zhengwu Liu, Kechao Tang, Wenyong Zhou, Ngai Wong

item.title: One Distribution, Two Channels: Coverage-Calibrated KV Retention and Compensation
item.description: arXiv:2610.02235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context decoding is increasingly constrained by key--value (KV) cache memory and bandwidth. Existing fixed-budget compression methods typically separate retention from compensation, while a retention ranking specifies neither discarded attention mass nor the direction of induced output error. We start from an exact factorization: eviction error equals evicted attention mass times the directional gap between the evicted centroid and retained output, highlighting the importance of set-level coverage in retention and mass-preserving memory writing. We introduce CORE COverage Calibration and Evicted-Mass REdistribution for KV Cache, which distills an offline allocation combining query utility and log-determinant coverage into a lightweight cache-aware indexer. At inference, one calibrated distribution drives both channels: its Top-$B$ ordering retains complementary KV states, while its excluded allocation mass and conditional weights parameterize latent-memory writes without a separate write-weight predictor or online log-determinant evaluation. Our analysis provides a four-term pre-compensation error certificate, characterizes non-additive coverage interactions, and establishes mass-independent write stability with hierarchical bounds through recurrent and query-adaptive normalization. Across three backbones, CORE exceeds the strongest RULER baseline by up to 3.78 points at 90% compression; LongBench and repeated-eviction evaluations further demonstrate strong effectiveness and decoding efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Shuxin Liu, Qing Liu, Yi Du, Ou Wu

item.title: Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.05062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference outside the design point of LLM serving systems. Although VLA architectures combine familiar vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, their runtime behavior in this batch-1 control setting remains uncharacterized. We characterize four representative VLA models on an edge GPU server and two onboard SoCs, using single-inference profiling and 43,200 closed-loop episodes. Action tensor dimensionality determines whether a stage is memory- or compute-bound, platform balance can shift that bottleneck, and GPU frequency scaling yields a platform-dependent energy-latency sweet spot. In closed-loop operation, overlapping inference with action execution creates an accuracy-speed-energy tradeoff, and no configuration is Pareto-dominant across deployment SLOs. These results guide joint design of VLA model architectures, hardware, and runtime policies.
item.dc:creator: Seonghun Jung, Sieun Moon, Jiyoung Jeong, Jimin Lee, Jaehyuk Huh

item.title: Leveraging SIMD for Accelerating Large-number Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2604.21566v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large-number arithmetic, widely used in scientific computing and cryptography, has seen limited adoption of single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) parallelism on modern CPUs due to the inherent dependencies in traditional algorithms. We present DigitsOnTurbo (DoT), which restructures the computation around independent, data-parallel operations, rather than vectorizing the standard algorithms, thereby leveraging the benefits provided by SIMD. Over prior SIMD implementations, DoT achieves up to 1.85x speedups for addition and subtraction, and 2.3x for multiplication. When integrated into state-of-the-art libraries (e.g., GMP, OpenSSL), DoT yields up to 4x speedup for addition and subtraction, and up to 2x speedup for multiplication, cascading into end-to-end throughput gains of up to 15.8% for scientific computations, and up to 5.6% latency and 6.2% throughput improvements on cryptographic implementations.
item.dc:creator: Subhrajit Das, Abhishek Bichhawat, Yuvraj Patel

item.title: Agentic Architect: An Agentic AI Framework for Architecture Design Exploration and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2604.25083v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Computer Architecture research has traditionally required the exploration of vast, highly complex design spaces through manual human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to accelerate this process by enabling fast and automated implementation and testing of different architectural mechanisms and their combinations. We introduce Agentic Architect, a framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design-space exploration and optimization. The Agentic Architect combines LLM-driven code evolution with cycle-accurate simulation and hardware cost modeling to explore performance, area, and power tradeoffs. Starting from a seed design, the LLM is prompted to explore the design space by implementing changes, guided by prior evaluation feedback. Each new design is compiled, simulated on training workloads, evaluated against the optimization objective, and constrained by area and power budgets. Its score and diagnostics update the candidate population and guide subsequent iterations. We evaluate the Agentic Architect framework across prefetching, cache replacement, and branch prediction. On 213 traces spanning five benchmark suites, its evolved prefetchers lead the evaluated L1D and L2 designs, delivering up to 6.7% and 2.6% additional speedup, respectively, over the strongest state-of-the-art design, while the best evolved cache replacement design improves over Mockingjay by up to 1.7%. Moreover, across 191 branch-prediction traces, the evolved branch predictor achieves 97.62% of TAGE-SC-L's geometric mean IPC at 10.58% of its area. Our analysis highlights the importance of seed selection, hardware constraints, and training workloads in shaping search outcomes. Overall, Agentic Architect establishes the first end-to-end framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design optimization, opening a new direction for architecture research.
item.dc:creator: Vasilis Kypriotis, Alexander Blasberg, Alexandros Moiras, Dimitrios Skarlatos
